title: Errors & suspense accounts
examples: When should I use a suspense account?
What is the difference between a compensating error and an error of principle?
Can I use a suspense account if I have multiple errors?

explain.say: Today we will learn about accounting errors and how to correct them.
An error of principle happens when you break an accounting rule.

draw.text: Error of Principle: Wrong rule used

explain.say: An error of commission is a simple mistake in recording a transaction.
An error of omission means you simply forgot to record a transaction.

draw.text: Error of Omission: Forgot to record

explain.say: A compensating error is when two or more errors cancel each other out.
In real life, if you pay a bill twice, that is an error of commission.

draw.text: Real Life: Paying a bill twice

faq.q: When is it appropriate to use a suspense account?
faq.a: You use a suspense account when your trial balance does not agree. It temporarily holds the difference until the error is found.
asks: What is the purpose of a suspense account?
Do I always need a suspense account?

faq.q: If the error is an error of principle, how do I fix it?
faq.a: You must pass a journal entry to correct the entry. This corrects the underlying accounting rule that was broken.
asks: How do I correct a principle error?
Does the suspense account fix principle errors?

faq.q: Can I correct an error of omission in the suspense account?
faq.a: Yes, if the omission affects the trial balance, you will use the suspense account to balance it initially. Then, a journal entry corrects the omission.
asks: What if I forget a whole transaction?
Is the suspense account for omissions?

faq.q: Does the suspense account show the actual error?
faq.a: No, it only shows the imbalance. The journal entry you pass reveals the actual nature of the error.
asks: What does the balance of the suspense account mean?
Does the suspense account tell me what went wrong?

faq.q: If the error is compensating, do I need a suspense account?
faq.a: No, if the errors perfectly cancel out, the trial balance will still balance, and you do not need a suspense account.
asks: If it balances, do I ignore the errors?
When is a suspense account unnecessary?

facts: A trial balance checks the arithmetic accuracy of the ledger.
An error of principle violates established accounting rules.
A suspense account is a temporary holding account.
Rectification entries are journal entries made to correct mistakes.

quiz.say: A business incorrectly debited a purchase expense to the machinery account. This is an example of:
quiz.why: This is wrong because it violates the fundamental rule of classifying expenses correctly.

wrong.0: This is wrong because we are looking at a single, isolated mistake.
wrong.2: This is tempting because it is a wrong posting, but the core issue is the rule violation, not just the posting.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the transaction was recorded, just in the wrong place.

quiz.say: If the total debits exceed the total credits by one hundred dollars, you would:

options.show: Credit the suspense account for one hundred dollars
options.say: Credit the suspense account for one hundred dollars

options.show: Debit the suspense account for one hundred dollars
options.say: Debit the suspense account for one hundred dollars

options.show: Do nothing, as the error will correct itself
options.say: Do nothing, as the error will correct itself

options.show: Use the error of commission account
options.say: Use the error of commission account

quiz.why: To make the total debits and credits equal, you must place the difference on the side that is currently lower.

wrong.1: This would make the imbalance worse, moving the difference to the wrong side.
wrong.2: Errors do not correct themselves; they must be actively rectified using journal entries.
wrong.3: The suspense account is the specific temporary account used to balance the trial balance.

quiz.say: A transaction was completely forgotten during the month's bookkeeping. This is best classified as:
quiz.why: Omission means the entire entry, debit and credit, was never made in the books.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the mistake is forgetting the entry, not using the wrong rule.
wrong.1: This is wrong because commission implies the entry was made, but incorrectly.
wrong.2: This is wrong because a single forgotten item cannot cancel out another error.
